tip: French is 'at the phone,' not on it: il est au téléphone. Au is à + le. The radio works the same way – à la radio.
English lets you drop 'that' – 'he says he's busy.' French never can: il dit qu'il est occupé. Que shortens to qu' before a vowel.
Un salon is a living room, not a hair salon: le dîner est servi dans le salon means dinner's served in the lounge.
French stays in the present with depuis: nous sommes amis depuis longtemps is literally 'we are friends since long' for 'we have been friends.'
Nationalities aren't capitalized in French when used as adjectives: vous êtes français, not Français.
A day 'passes itself' in French: comment s'est passée ta journée. Se passer means to happen, and it takes être in the past.
Laisser plus an adjective means to leave something in a state: a laissé la fenêtre ouverte = left the window open. Ouverte agrees with fenêtre.
After sans, French uses the plain verb, not the -ing form: sans dire au revoir = without saying goodbye.
Animé means lively or bustling, not 'animated': les rues sont animées describes busy, buzzing streets.
French flavors things with à, not 'of': une tarte aux pommes is an apple tart. Aux is à + les – literally 'a tart with the apples.'
You HAVE your age in French: mon fils a trois ans is literally 'my son has three years.' Never use être for age.
De marks which train by its time: le train de huit heures = the eight o'clock train. It's 'the train of eight hours.'
Aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait is literally 'as soon as said, as soon as done' – the French for 'no sooner said than done.'
Le monde means 'people' here, not 'the world': tellement de monde = so many people. It stays singular, so the verb is est venu.
Time uses an empty 'il': il est midi = it's noon. Midi is one word for the twelve o'clock midday – minuit is midnight.
Long becomes longue for a feminine noun, gaining u and e: la route est longue, not longe.
L'addition is the restaurant bill, not a math sum: tu as payé l'addition = did you pay the bill?
France runs on the 24-hour clock: vingt heures is 8 PM, literally 'twenty hours.' Vingt et une heures would be 9 PM.
Regarder already means 'look at,' so no preposition follows: tu as regardé le film = you watched the film, never regardé à.
Attendre swallows the 'for': j'ai attendu le train = I waited for the train. Adding pour here would be wrong.
Chercher already contains the 'for': il a cherché ses clés = he looked for his keys. Never add pour after it.
After quelque chose, French links the adjective with de and keeps it masculine: quelque chose de bon = something good.
You don't 'pass' an exam in French, you succeed at it: tu as réussi ton examen = you passed your exam.
Feminine countries take en for 'in' or 'to': en Espagne = in Spain. No article – it's not 'dans l'Espagne.'
Entrer needs dans before a place: il est entré dans la pièce = he entered the room. And it takes être, not avoir, in the past.
You climb 'into' a vehicle in French: elle est montée dans le taxi = she got into the taxi. Monter takes être here.
Téléphoner needs à before the person: il a téléphoné à son frère = he called his brother. You phone 'to' someone in French.
Mou means soft or squishy: le canapé est mou. It's an oddball – its feminine is molle, not moue.
Qu'est-ce qui asks 'what' as the subject, the thing doing the action: qu'est-ce qui s'est passé = what happened. Use qu'est-ce que when 'what' is the object.
Des shrinks to de when an adjective comes before the noun: de nouvelles recettes, not des nouvelles recettes.
Profiter de means to make the most of, not just profit: nous avons profité du beau temps = we enjoyed the nice weather. Du is de + le.
Changer de takes no article: elle a changé de travail = she changed jobs. It's 'changed of job,' same with changer de train.
Chez plus a person means at their place: il est resté chez lui = he stayed at his home. There's no single English word for it.
Homework is always plural in French: mes devoirs. Le devoir on its own means duty – the plural shifts it to schoolwork.
Nouveau turns into nouvel before a vowel sound, for smoothness: un nouvel appartement, not un nouveau appartement.
Garder les enfants means to babysit, literally 'to keep the children': elle a gardé les enfants de sa voisine.
You 'walk' the dog with promener: tu as promené le chien. It means to take out for a walk – you're walking it, not strolling yourself.
Commencer links to the next verb with à: a commencé à lire = started to read. The à is required before the infinitive.
Finir attaches to the next verb with de: j'ai fini de manger = I finished eating. Different verbs pick à or de – finir takes de.
Eu, the past participle of avoir, is pronounced just like the letter u – the e is silent: nous avons eu = we had.
A few adjectives sit before the noun: les grands arbres = the tall trees. Size, age, and beauty words like grand usually lead.
Une place is a seat or spot here, not just a 'place': deux places pour le concert = two seats for the concert.
Commander means to order food, not to command: nous avons commandé des pizzas = we ordered pizzas.
Quantity words take plain de, never du or de la: assez d'eau = enough water. Same for beaucoup d'eau, trop d'eau.
